newsitem.title: FRANCE: France reveals scale of EMU deficit woes.
newsitem.headline: France reveals scale of EMU deficit woes.

text.p: A French government source said on Friday "first signs" showed the public deficit could top 3.4-3.5 percent of gross domestic product this year but everything would be done to launch a European single currency on time in 1999.

It was too early to say now where the deficit would stand at the end of 1997 but France's new left-wing government had in any case always stressed that the Maastricht treaty on monetary union did not set a strict three percent goal, the source said.
What would count when European Union leaders met next spring to decide who joined the single currency was the "trend" towards three percent measured across 1997 and 1998, the source said.

The estimate, still very tentative, according to the source, comes on the heels of confirmation by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Thursday that France's deficit was not falling to the strict 3.0 percent goal, or even 3.1 percent, this year.

"What we know already is there was slippage in the early part of the year, which puts us a little beyond 3.4-3.5 percent, but these are only first indications," the source said. "You have to be very careful with estimates at this stage."

The source said the decisions next year on who participates in the single currency launch would be taken "on the basis of 1997 and the trend of 1998" and the France would do "everything in its power" to meet its commitment to join on time in 1999.

The source said Germany -- France's principal ally in the European union project but traditionally a disciple of a rigid "three percent" interpretation of the Maastricht deficit goal -- had budget troubles of its own.
The aim, he said, "was not to do worse than our neighbours." "Our aim is to remain more or less in line."
"We will not to get to three percent (in 1997) but it is certain that we are on the path toward reducing public deficits from 1997," the source said.
"What is reasonable is that there be truly reasonable headway." The stress would be on the trend across 1997 and 1998.
"1997 and 1998 are not separate, the evaluation has to be made across 1997-1998," the source said, highlighting there was considerable time left between now and the EMU launch decisions.
There was a "narrow but manageable" margin for manoeuvre in terms of France's budget but no decisions had been taken yet on how to proceed.

Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, whose government was swept to power in a June 1 election, campaigned against imposing further austerity to qualify for monetary union but has told his ministers that they must not let spending rise.

After only a few weeks in power it is confronted with the unenviable task of balancing a promise to make employment its top priority and to fuel extra growth without adding to the cutbacks imposed by the previous centre-right government.
Jospin said in his maiden parliamentary speech on June 19 that the country's finances were in a "serious" state.
He has commissioned an independent audit of public finances for completion by July 21 and the government is holding off on major budget decisions until after the summer recess.

The government source who spoke on Friday played down press reports that it already had plans for company tax increases in the pipeline but acknowledged that "some savings would have to be considered" if the situation turned out worse than expected.

The emphasis would be on ensuring that interest rates were kept low and foreign exchange rates maintained at current levels to promote investment and improve the growth rate and employment, which would also help deficit control.

Part of the strategy included "rebalancing" the tax burden between households and companies but the government was still at the stage of general policy. On specific measures in this area it would proceed cautiously and was conscious of the need to protect small companies, he said.
